A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Rashomon-set study. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original decision-tree experiments on six datasets, simulations using five synthetic distributions, and appendix studies of stability, sampling strategies, and individual-model vulnerability.

after.justification: v2 retains these results and adds original simultaneous-attack, neural-network, membership-inference, and AwA2 attack-transferability evaluations.

M1.justification: The central Rashomon-set approach and existing tree-selection procedures remain. Section 6.4 and Appendices E.6–E.8 add an auxiliary disclosure procedure: choose the smaller of a privacy-constrained model count and a Kneedle-derived knee count. v1 only discussed a possible disclosure sweet spot.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained six tabular datasets and synthetic distributions, v2 evaluates Iris, Seeds, and Wine, and adds image/concept classification on AwA2. It also introduces membership-inference evaluation and simultaneous attacks targeting multiple released trees, substantially broadening tasks and threat scenarios.

E2.justification: The existing tree-selection comparators are retained. v2 adds an explicit comparison between simultaneous multi-model attacks and Kantchelian et al.'s single-model attack in Figure 17, alongside reference-model accuracy and random-guessing controls in the new neural-network experiments.

E3.justification: The original TreeFARMS/DRAFT settings remain. New protocols include joint-region attack searches over up to ten trees, AWP-estimated neural Rashomon sets with specified relative loss tolerances, FGSM evaluations, and Yeom membership-inference error. AwA2 evaluation introduces ten pretrained models and ten-step PGD with an 8/255 budget and 2/255 step size.

E4.justification: v2 adds clean-versus-adversarial accuracy analysis, simultaneous-attack robustness tests, neural-network sensitivity to attack strength, and quantitative disclosure-knee/privacy-constraint analyses. These investigate additional robustness mechanisms and operational trade-offs; the earlier stability, sparsity, and sampling-strategy studies are retained.

E5.justification: Existing five-fold and five-run tree reporting remains. Figures 20–21 specify twenty seeded trials and standard deviations for new neural-network experiments, while Figure 23 adds linear-fit slopes and R-squared reporting. These are additional reporting procedures, not evidence of increased repetitions for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: The original tree and simulation results are retained, while v2 adds substantial simultaneous-attack, neural-network, membership-inference, and disclosure-selection results. Its new AwA2 Table 7 reports 43.95% source-model versus 61.68% transfer-target task accuracy, a 17.73-percentage-point recovery. These are newly reported evaluations, not matched-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v1's one-feature rule-list vulnerability claim becomes Theorem 4.2 with conjunctive-antecedent and nonempty-leaf assumptions and a general l+I−1 attack budget. v2 also adds a total-variation version of the ensemble distribution bound and Theorem C.5 linking approximation gains to convex-hull diversity, and corrects an inequality in the distribution-shift proof.

C1.justification: The central robustness–privacy trade-off and stability claims persist. The introduction replaces the guarantee that diversity prevents attack transfer with a claim of reduced transfer risk, and newly claims empirical extension to more complex neural architectures. These refine and broaden the retained thesis.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes attacked-input disagreement from the clean-data proxy and explicitly disclaims guarantees against all adaptive attacks. It revises the reconstruction-versus-membership discussion, qualifies neural membership leakage as potentially nonmonotonic, explains simultaneous-attack limitations, and develops efficiency-limited versus privacy-limited disclosure regimes beyond v1's qualitative sweet-spot discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, dataset row/feature counts, neural architecture and Rashomon-tolerance details, and attack configurations. It documents reuse of ten pretrained RashomonCBMs without additional training and an NVIDIA RTX A5000 for their evaluation. These substantially expand reproducibility information without implying changes to retained tree settings.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially updates the literature and positioning. It explicitly distinguishes this set-level analysis from Hsu et al. (2026)'s individual-model trustworthiness study and frames its defense perspective against Yao et al. (2025)'s attack-transferability analysis. Additional works cover concept-based networks, robustness definitions, and privacy attacks.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting and compression, including replacement of the enumerated contribution list. v2 reorganizes the appendices, adds a results-navigation section and operationalization subsections, and revises terminology and explanatory passages throughout.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and references, relocates the conceptual comparison table and KL plot, and recomposes main-text figures while retaining their fuller appendix versions. It adds numerous analysis plots and summary/result tables, including neural-network panels, AwA2 results, and annotated disclosure curves.

improvement.justification: v2 repairs important theoretical weaknesses through the revised rule-list assumptions and corrected distribution-shift proof. Its simultaneous-attack and neural/image evaluations substantially strengthen evidence beyond v1's single-target tree experiments, while added implementation information improves reproducibility. The new disclosure guidance has a limitation: its illustrative 35% tolerance does not establish the statistical privacy assurance claimed in Appendix E.8. Nevertheless, the improvements to mathematical validity and empirical support are substantial.
